title: The unseen
hookLine: believing in what isn't seen is where faith starts (2:3)

lines: A SIGNAL, A PILOT, THE AIR.
cards: A short list of things you trusted today without seeing them. The signal that carried your messages. The pilot of a plane you heard overhead.
The person who cooked food you bought. The air in the room, which you breathed several hundred times and never once looked at. Trust in what you can't see isn't strange.
Nobody gets through a Tuesday without it. And when the Qur'an describes the people it's meant for, on its second page, the very first quality it names is exactly that.

teach.b: Al-Baqarah begins by calling the book a guidance for those who keep their duty, and then describes them. Verse three, in Pickthall's translation, starts: "Who believe in the Unseen."
Before prayer, before giving, the first thing named is what they trust. The Arabic is al-ghayb.
The root gh-y-b means to be absent, hidden from view; a student who misses class is gha'ib, absent. So the unseen isn't the imaginary. It's what is real but not in front of you.

A well-known hadith in Sahih Muslim, where Jibril comes as a stranger and questions the Prophet, lists the heart of faith: Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the measuring out of good and bad.
Almost all of it sits in the unseen. And the Qur'an is honest about who holds it.
Surah six says that with Allah are the keys of the unseen, and no one knows them but Him. It adds a small, startling picture: not a leaf falls but He knows it.
Surah twenty-seven says no one in the heavens or the earth knows the unseen except Allah.

teach.h: TRUST IT, DON'T CLAIM TO SEE IT.
teach.b: That's why classical scholars were firm about fortune-tellers: a hadith in Sahih Muslim warns that whoever consults one to ask about hidden things has their prayer unaccepted for forty nights.
So faith in the unseen has two sides. It trusts what can't be seen. And it doesn't pretend to see it.
The future, the hidden, the leaf before it falls: those stay with Allah.

how: Muslims describe faith (iman) as belief in Allah, the angels, the revealed books, the messengers, the Last Day and divine decree, much of it in the unseen; classical scholars warned against fortune-telling as a claim on what only Allah knows.

o: what is imagined and not truly real
the far future, which can be foretold
what is real but hidden from view

p: the unseen, real but out of view
the first quality: belief in the unseen
the keys of the unseen are with Allah

s: it means absent, hidden from view: real, but not in front of you.
belief in the unseen is the first quality al-Baqarah names
verse three, before prayer and giving.
the Qur'an says some people can read the unseen
it says no one in the heavens or the earth knows the unseen except Allah.

games.q: a friend offers to take you to someone who can tell your future. what do the classical sources say?
o: go, if it's just for fun.
a hadith warns against it: the unseen belongs to Allah.
it's fine if you also pray.
games.why: a hadith in Sahih Muslim warns that consulting a fortune-teller about hidden things leaves one's prayer unaccepted for forty nights.

practice: Close your eyes so the seen goes quiet, and feel your breath coming in: you can't see the air, but you're living on it.
Pick one unseen thing to rest your weight on for the rest of this sit: your breath, someone's love for you, or, if you believe, Allah's care. Don't try to picture it; just lean on it.

wordCard.voice: The unseen. Al-ghayb, from gh-y-b, absent: what is real but out of view, the first thing named in al-Baqarah's picture of faith. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the unseen, from gh-y-b, to be absent.

carryVoice: Your line: faith in the unseen. The keys stay with the One who holds them. Day six hundred sixty-six.
